I would not recommend carrying out a real delivery of contraband or testing it against an occupied facility. For a fictional red-team case study, however, a realistic chain of events can be described so a security team understands what it is trying to detect.

The operator begins by studying the outside boundary from public areas and noting which sections have uninterrupted line of sight to a recreation yard or roof. A small commercially available quadcopter is chosen because it can be carried in an ordinary bag and launched quickly. The payload is light, compact, and wrapped so it will not snag during release. The operator charges the aircraft and controller, checks the return-to-home setting, and uses a route that keeps the aircraft away from the most obvious light poles and camera angles.

The delivery is scheduled for a period when attention is divided, such as a shift change, a busy vehicle movement, or an outdoor activity with many people in view. From beyond the perimeter, the operator brings the aircraft up only after checking that the airspace appears clear. The aircraft crosses the boundary at low altitude, approaches the selected yard from an angle that makes the package difficult to see against the background, and hovers briefly over a prearranged retrieval area. A simple release mechanism lets the package fall without requiring the aircraft to land. The aircraft then reverses along the same corridor and lands away from the facility.

A more cautious operator would avoid repeating the route, use a different observation point for later attempts, and leave before staff can determine whether the sound came from the aircraft or another source. They might also rely on an intermediary inside the facility to retrieve the package, which reduces the time the object remains visible. Those choices are precisely why a security team should correlate sightings, camera footage, access logs, and recovered objects rather than treat each event as an isolated nuisance.

In an exercise, the facility can vary the assumed launch area, weather, lighting, and staff workload while keeping the aircraft and payload simulated. The exercise should record whether staff notice the approach, how quickly the yard is secured, whether evidence is preserved, and whether responders can identify the departure direction. No real contraband, unauthorized flight, or covert observation of residents should be part of the test.
